V01.root_cause: Trunk between SW1 and SW2 is not carrying VLAN 20
V01.evidence: show interfaces trunk lists 'Vlans allowed on trunk: 1,10' — VLAN 20 is absent
V01.next_command: show vlan brief (confirm VLAN 20 exists and is active on both switches)
fix_steps: On SW1, run: switchport trunk allowed vlan add 20
Repeat on SW2 if the same restriction exists there
Re-check show interfaces trunk for VLAN 20
Re-test PC-A to PC-B connectivity

V02.root_cause: Fa0/5 access port assigned to VLAN 99 instead of the intended VLAN 10
V02.evidence: show interfaces fa0/5 switchport shows 'Access Mode VLAN: 99'
V02.next_command: show vlan brief (confirm VLAN 10 exists and what else is on VLAN 99)
fix_steps: switchport access vlan 10 on Fa0/5
Verify VLAN 10 SVI/gateway is reachable
Re-test PC connectivity

V03.root_cause: Trunk between SW1 and SW2 is not fully configured
V03.evidence: CDP log shows a native VLAN mismatch warning between the switches
V03.next_command: show interfaces trunk on both switches
fix_steps: Re-run switchport mode trunk on both ends
Confirm the trunk comes up
Re-test connectivity
V03.wrong_reason: AI treated the CDP native-VLAN-mismatch message as a generic 'trunk not configured' problem. The trunk IS up and passing traffic — the actual issue is the native VLAN differs (1 vs 99) between the two ends, which needs 'switchport trunk native vlan 1' matched on both sides, not re-enabling trunking.

V04.root_cause: VLAN 30 does not exist in the VLAN database
V04.evidence: show vlan brief lists VLANs 1, 10, 20 — VLAN 30 is missing entirely
fix_steps: vlan 30 / name Finance in global config
Assign the correct ports to VLAN 30
Confirm VLAN 30 appears in show vlan brief
Re-test PC connectivity

G01.root_cause: PC's default gateway is set to 192.168.10.100 instead of the router's 192.168.10.1
G01.evidence: PC ipconfig shows Default Gateway: 192.168.10.100, which does not match the router sub-interface .1
G01.next_command: show ip interface brief on the router to confirm .1 is correct
fix_steps: Correct the PC's default gateway to 192.168.10.1
Renew DHCP or set static IP correctly
Re-test connectivity outside the subnet

G02.root_cause: VLAN 20 sub-interface on the router is administratively down
G02.evidence: show ip interface brief shows Gi0/0.20 status 'administratively down'
fix_steps: Enter interface g0/0.20, run 'no shutdown'
Confirm status changes to up/up
Re-test VLAN 20 connectivity

G03.root_cause: R1 is completely down and no backup gateway is configured
G03.evidence: show standby brief shows Active as R1(unreachable)
fix_steps: Restore R1 power/connectivity
Confirm HSRP re-converges once R1 is back
G03.wrong_reason: The AI assumed HSRP was entirely unconfigured on R2, but the evidence actually shows HSRP IS running and R2 correctly went to Standby — it just never becomes Active because preempt is disabled on R2. The fix is 'standby 1 preempt' on R2, not just waiting for R1 to come back.

G04.root_cause: VLAN 40 SVI has no IP address configured
G04.evidence: show ip interface brief shows Vlan40 IP-Address: unassigned
fix_steps: Assign the intended IP (e.g. 192.168.40.1/24) to interface vlan40
Confirm status shows up/up with the correct IP
Re-test PC connectivity to the gateway

D01.root_cause: Router interface for VLAN 30 is missing 'ip helper-address', so DHCP broadcasts never reach the central server
D01.evidence: show run interface g0/0.30 has no ip helper-address line
D01.next_command: show ip dhcp binding on the DHCP server to confirm no VLAN 30 leases exist
fix_steps: Add 'ip helper-address <DHCP-server-IP>' under g0/0.30
Release/renew DHCP on an affected PC
Confirm the PC gets a valid VLAN 30 address

D02.root_cause: DHCP pool address range is exhausted
D02.evidence: show ip dhcp pool shows 30 leased addresses against a pool sized for 30 hosts
fix_steps: Expand the pool's network size, or
Clear stale/expired leases with clear ip dhcp binding *
Confirm new PCs successfully lease an address

D03.root_cause: DHCP pool is running low on available addresses
D03.evidence: A duplicate address conflict was reported involving the gateway IP
fix_steps: Expand the DHCP pool range
Monitor for further conflicts
D03.wrong_reason: The AI defaulted to 'pool exhaustion' as a generic explanation for an address conflict, but the real evidence is that the gateway address itself was never excluded from the pool ('ip dhcp excluded-address' missing), so DHCP handed it out to a client. Expanding the pool would not fix — and could worsen — this.

D04.root_cause: DHCP pool configured with a /28 mask instead of the intended /24, so clients calculate the wrong subnet and can't reach the .1 gateway
D04.evidence: ip dhcp pool network line shows 255.255.255.240 (/28) while the LAN is documented as /24
fix_steps: Correct the network statement to 255.255.255.0
Clear existing bad leases
Re-test PC connectivity to the gateway

N01.root_cause: DHCP is handing out a public DNS resolver (8.8.8.8) instead of the internal DNS server
N01.evidence: PC ipconfig /all shows DNS Servers: 8.8.8.8; DHCP pool dns-server line also points to 8.8.8.8
fix_steps: Update the DHCP pool's dns-server line to the internal DNS IP (192.168.1.53)
Release/renew DHCP on the PC
Re-test resolving fileserver.local

N02.root_cause: Internal DNS server service is down or unreachable
N02.evidence: nslookup times out against 192.168.1.53 for every client, and the DNS server process is not responding
N02.next_command: Check DNS service status directly on the DNS server host
fix_steps: Restart the DNS service on the server
Confirm the server host is reachable (ping, then nslookup)
Re-test resolution from a client

N03.root_cause: Client is missing its DNS suffix, so short (unqualified) hostnames cannot be completed into an FQDN
N03.evidence: ipconfig /all shows Connection-specific DNS Suffix: (none), while the full FQDN resolves fine
fix_steps: Set the DNS suffix to corp.local on the client (or push via DHCP option 15)
Re-test the short hostname lookup

N04.root_cause: Client is statically configured to use an external DNS resolver instead of the internal DNS server
N04.evidence: ipconfig /all shows DNS Servers: 1.1.1.1 and DHCP Enabled: No
fix_steps: Switch the adapter back to DHCP, or manually set DNS to 192.168.1.53
Re-test resolving an internal hostname

R01.root_cause: HQ router (R1) has no return route to the branch subnet 10.20.0.0/24
R01.evidence: show ip route on R1 has no entry for 10.20.0.0/24
R01.next_command: show run | section router or show ip route on R2 for comparison
fix_steps: Add ip route 10.20.0.0 255.255.255.0 <branch-next-hop> on R1
Confirm the route appears in show ip route
Re-test HQ-to-branch connectivity

R02.root_cause: OSPF is not fully enabled on one of the two router interfaces
R02.evidence: Neighbor stuck in EXSTART state between R1 and R2
fix_steps: Re-check the network statements enabling OSPF on both interfaces
Re-verify neighbor state
R02.wrong_reason: OSPF IS enabled on both sides — that's why a neighbor relationship formed at all and progressed to EXSTART. Sticking at EXSTART/EXCHANGE with no other symptom is the classic signature of an MTU mismatch (1500 vs 1400 in the evidence), not a missing network statement. Re-checking network statements would find nothing wrong and waste review time.

R03.root_cause: Static route to 172.16.30.0/24 uses the wrong exit interface (Serial0/0/0 instead of Serial0/0/1)
R03.evidence: show run shows the static route pointing out Serial0/0/0, but the topology note says 172.16.30.0/24 is reachable via Serial0/0/1
fix_steps: Remove the incorrect static route
Re-test connectivity to 172.16.30.0/24

R04.root_cause: EIGRP autonomous system numbers do not match between R1 (100) and R2 (200)
R04.evidence: show ip protocols on R1 shows 'eigrp 100', on R2 shows 'eigrp 200'
R04.next_command: show ip eigrp neighbors on both routers
fix_steps: Standardize both routers on the same EIGRP AS number
Confirm a neighbor relationship forms
Confirm routes are learned on both sides

A01.root_cause: A deny statement for TCP port 80 sits above the intended permit in ACL 101, blocking the traffic due to first-match processing
A01.evidence: show access-lists 101 line 10 denies tcp any any eq 80 before line 20 permits it to the server
A01.next_command: show access-lists 101 (confirm hit counters on line 10)
fix_steps: Remove or reorder the deny statement so the permit is evaluated first
Re-apply/verify the ACL
Re-test HTTP access to the server

A02.root_cause: ACL 105 is applied outbound instead of inbound on Gi0/1, blocking return traffic
A02.evidence: show ip interface gi0/1 shows 'Outgoing access list is 105' and 'Inbound access list is not set'
fix_steps: Remove the ACL from the outbound direction
Apply it in the correct direction per its intent
Re-test client-to-server request/response

A03.root_cause: ACL 10 is applied in the wrong direction on the interface toward the HR server
A03.evidence: ACL 10 denies 192.168.50.0/24 and is applied on the interface toward the HR server
fix_steps: Re-check inbound vs outbound application of ACL 10
Re-test connectivity
A03.wrong_reason: Direction wasn't the problem — ACL 10 is a standard ACL, which can only match on source address, not destination. Applied anywhere near that interface, it blocks 192.168.50.0/24 from everything, not just the HR server. The real fix is replacing it with an extended ACL that matches both source (192.168.50.0/24) and destination (the HR server), not changing direction.

A04.root_cause: No explicit permit entry exists for the new Finance subnet (192.168.60.0/24) in ACL 110, so it falls into the implicit deny
A04.evidence: show access-lists 110 only has permit entries for 192.168.10.0/24 and 192.168.20.0/24
A04.next_command: show access-lists 110 (confirm hit count on implicit deny)
fix_steps: Re-verify ACL order (new line lands before implicit deny)
Re-test Finance subnet access to the file server

T01.root_cause: 'ip nat inside' was never applied to the LAN-facing interface (Gi0/0), so no traffic is marked for translation
T01.evidence: show ip nat translations is empty; Gi0/0 is missing 'ip nat inside' while Gi0/1 correctly has 'ip nat outside'
fix_steps: Apply 'ip nat inside' under interface Gi0/0
Re-test internet access from an internal PC
Confirm entries appear in show ip nat translations

T02.root_cause: Static NAT maps the public IP to the wrong internal address (192.168.1.99 instead of the server's real 192.168.1.100)
T02.evidence: show run shows 'ip nat inside source static 192.168.1.99 203.0.113.10', but the web server is documented at .100
fix_steps: Remove the incorrect static NAT entry
Add: ip nat inside source static 192.168.1.100 203.0.113.10
Re-test external access to the web server

T03.root_cause: NAT overload's outside address pool has been exhausted
T03.evidence: Some hosts on 192.168.1.192/27 cannot reach the internet while the rest of the office can
fix_steps: Add a second public IP to the NAT pool
Re-test affected hosts
T03.wrong_reason: PAT overload on a single interface IP doesn't run out the way a NAT pool does — thousands of port translations are available. The actual evidence is that ACL 1 (which decides who gets translated at all) only permits 192.168.1.0/26, so the .192/27 hosts are never even considered for translation. Adding a public IP would not fix a problem that's really an incomplete ACL.

W01.root_cause: Guest WLAN is mapped to the management interface instead of an isolated VLAN, and no ACL enforces isolation
W01.evidence: show wlan on the WLC shows the Guest profile's interface set to 'management' with no ACL applied
fix_steps: Create a dedicated guest VLAN/interface
Re-map the Guest WLAN to it
Apply an ACL blocking guest-to-internal traffic
Re-test that a guest device cannot reach the internal server

W02.root_cause: Pre-shared key mismatch between the AP and the client (case-sensitive passphrase typed incorrectly)
W02.evidence: AP config shows passphrase 'CorpWifi2024!' while the client profile has 'CorpWiFi2024!' (differing capitalization)
W02.next_command: show wlan security wpa on the AP; compare exact passphrase case with the client profile
fix_steps: Have the user delete and re-add the Wi-Fi profile with the exact correct passphrase
Confirm successful association and DHCP lease

W03.root_cause: AP1 and AP2 are both set to 2.4GHz channel 6 with overlapping coverage, causing co-channel interference
W03.evidence: show controllers dot11Radio 0 on both AP1 and AP2 reports Channel: 6
W03.next_command: show controllers dot11Radio 0 | include Channel (on all nearby APs)
fix_steps: Change AP2 to a non-overlapping channel (e.g. 1 or 11)
Confirm the change on show controllers dot11Radio 0
Re-test signal stability near the east wall
